To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the screening participation of women aged 70 to 75 years increased from 1999 to 2000; the breast cancer detection rates in women aged 70 and above increased strongly from 1998 through 2000, and that the detection rate of breast cancer in women aged 74 to 75 years in 2000 is close to the detection rate that would be expected on the basis of a simulation model assuming an increase in the sojourn duration of breast cancer with age.

(1) the attendance of women aged 70 to 75 years in the Dutch breast cancer mammography screening programme has increased from 1996 to 2000, and that the attendance of women 75 years of aged has increased the most; (2) the detection rate of breast cancer in women aged 70-75 years increased with age; (3) the detection rate in women aged 75 years was close to that simulated by a model assuming a continuously increasing sojourning time

the screening participation in women aged 70-75 is high, that the detection rate increases with age, that the detection rates in this age group are close to the predicted values assuming a continuously increasing sojourning time, that the detection to referral rate ratio increases with age, and that this ratio is close to the ratio in women aged 55-69.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether screening for breast cancer in women aged 70 to 75 years can still be regarded as beneficial.
the question whether the upper age limit of 75 years of the women invited in the Dutch breast cancer programme is appropriate.
the question of whether it is appropriate to invite women up to the age of 75 years.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Dutch breast screening programme for women in the age range 70–74 years has a high participation, and a high sensitivity and specificity.
the Dutch programme should be continued for women aged 50 to 75, with the upper age limit of invitation being set at 75 years.
the Dutch screening programme is still very effective and that the age limit for invitation should be 75 years, at present.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the upper age limit for Dutch breast cancer screening is appropriate.
the Dutch breast cancer population‐based screening programme for women 50–75 is effective and safe, and the upper age limit of 75 can be considered as a reasonable choice.
the Dutch programme is very successful, but the age limit of 75 years for the women invited should be reconsidered.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sojourn‐time of breast cancer increases steadily with age beyond the age of about 65 years.
women aged 75 years can be considered to be a suitable age group for population‐based breast cancer screening.
the screening attendance among women aged 70 to 75 is high and the detection rates are comparable with those of younger women.
